extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, legal scholars, law students, and policymakers interested in US patentable subject matter (especially business-methods)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether claimed inventions—especially business methods and financial methods—are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 in light of Bilski, State Street, and related doctrine. Focuses on interpretive approaches (textualism), judicially-created exceptions, statutory-structure arguments, and multi-factor/criteria-based analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textualist statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret §101 (and related Patent Act provisions) by using the ordinary, contemporary, common meaning of the statutory words and avoid 'reading in' limitations that the legislature has not expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues the Court's shift toward textualism (citing Chakrabarty, Diehr, JEM Ag Supply) explains acceptance of business-method patents: Congress used expansive terms (modified by 'any'), so courts should give §101 wide scope and not impose judge-made exceptions unless tied to the text. Textualists emphasize focusing the inquiry on the statute's language rather than importing extra-statutory triple-word tests or policy preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize judicial exceptions: laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior Supreme Court precedents provide three specific exceptions to §101’s broad patent-eligibility principles: 'laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although these exceptions are acknowledged not to be required by the statutory text, Bilski tied them to the statute by linking them to the requirement that a patentable process must be 'new and useful.' The exceptions have governed the statute as a matter of stare decisis for well over a century. Analysts should treat these categories as controlling limits that must be reconciled with textualist reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject nonstatutory triple-word tests as exclusive rules (UCT/TSM/MOT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests such as the 'useful, concrete, and tangible' (UCT), the 'teaching-suggestion-motivation' (TSM), and the 'machine-or-transformation' (MOT) are judge-made, nonstatutory triple-word tests that the Supreme Court has been skeptical of or rejected as exclusive standards for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a textualist perspective the basic objection to these tests is their lack of connection to the statute. The Court in Bilski refused to endorse State Street's UCT test and has cautioned against adopting rigid nonstatutory rules. These tests may be informative historically or analytically but should not be treated as the controlling statutory standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards-based, multi-factor 'criteria' approach (weigh factors, don't decide by single factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple criteria or factors, weighed together, in determining patentable subject matter rather than imposing a single bright-line rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski’s majority invited the Federal Circuit and the PTO to develop 'limiting criteria' that further the purposes of the Patent Act and are not inconsistent with its text. The PTO's post-Bilski guidance explicitly framed its points as 'factors [to be] weighed in making the determination' and warned that 'it would be improper to make a conclusion based on one factor while ignoring other factors.' Criteria should be applied in combination and tied back to statutory text and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality/abstractness (claims that are 'so abstract and sweeping')
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claimed invention embodies a 'general concept' presented in such an abstract and sweeping way that it covers both known and unknown uses of the concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO identified this as a factor. The article notes that extremely general concept-claims are likely not 'new' or 'useful' at the statutory level, may be incompatible with §112 requirements for 'clear, concise, and exact terms' and particularity, and may therefore be treated as abstract ideas excluded from §101. Example: Bilski's high-level hedging concept was characterized as a fundamental economic practice long prevalent in commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie §101 analysis to other Patent Act provisions (structural/textual arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the text and structure of the whole Patent Act—especially §§ 112 (written description/definiteness), 102 (novelty), and 103 (nonobviousness)—when assessing §101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A textualist analysis can legitimately ask whether the invention is such that other statutory requirements can be meaningfully applied. If a claimed invention is so abstract that statutory requirements (e.g., precise claiming under §112, novelty under §102, nonobviousness under §103) cannot be rationally applied, then the structure of the Act supports excluding it from §101. Thus §101 eligibility should reflect whether the claim's 'true merits' (new, useful, nonobvious, precisely described, definitely claimed) can be evaluated under the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emerging_field_rigor (fit within a developing scientific/engineering field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claimed invention fits within an emerging or established field (e.g., financial engineering) that provides rigorous terminology and standards for identifying and defining new contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim lies within a maturing field with robust prior art and technical standards, it is more likely to be sustained as patentable; by contrast, methods that are merely general advice or practices without a rigorous disciplinary foundation (e.g., 'How to Win Friends and Influence People') are unlikely to be patent-eligible. Claimants seeking Supreme Court validation for business-method patents must demonstrate the emergence of such rigorous fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete machine vs. abstract process distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish claims directed to physical machines/systems from claims directed to abstract processes or methods; machines for doing business are more readily acceptable than pure abstract methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Stevens acknowledged that State Street’s claims might be patentable because they were directed to machines rather than processes. The Court historically treats tangible machines differently than abstract practices; claims to concrete machines combining hardware and software may survive scrutiny that pure method claims would not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prior-art/practicality indicators (long-prevalent, well-known, taught in introductory classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claimed idea is a 'fundamental economic practice long prevalent in our system of commerce', 'well-known', or taught in introductory classes—indicators that the claim may be an abstract idea or obvious/anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski used such factual characterizations of the claimed hedging practice to support finding the claim abstract and unpatentable. These indicators cut against novelty and nonobviousness and support exclusion under §101 when the claim merely recites longstanding commercial practices or commonplace techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie criteria rigorously back to statutory text and stare decisis when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When articulating limiting criteria or factors, ground them in the Patent Act's text and in controlling precedent rather than relying on policy preferences or ad hoc tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses that a textualist-minded court will expect criteria to be justified by statute or structure; where exceptions survive, courts may rely on stare decisis to maintain them but still seek a textualist rationale (as Bilski attempted by linking exceptions to 'new and useful'). PTO and courts should therefore connect any factors to statutory provisions (e.g., §§101, 102, 103, 112) or established precedent.
